## Q1
Match List-I (Algorithm design techniques) with List-II.

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| A. Dynamic programming | I. Floyd Warshall shortest path |
| B. Greedy | II. Huffman coding |
| C. Back tracking | III. Hamiltonian cycle problem |
| D. Branch and bound | IV. Travelling salesman (TSP) using lower bound |

## Q1 - Options
(A) A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I
(B) A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I
(C) A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV
(D) A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

## Q1 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Greedy Algorithms & Dynamic Programming
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q24

Each algorithmic technique is best illustrated by one of its classic applications.

A-I — The Floyd-Warshall all-pairs shortest path algorithm is a textbook dynamic programming algorithm, building solutions from smaller subproblems.

B-II — Huffman coding greedily merges the two lowest-frequency nodes at each step, making it a classic greedy algorithm.

C-III — The Hamiltonian cycle problem is classically solved by backtracking, building a path and abandoning a branch as soon as it cannot be extended.

D-IV — The travelling salesman problem, when solved by pruning partial tours using a computed lower bound, is a standard branch-and-bound application.

A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV is therefore the correct match.

## Q2
Which of the following are limitations of Greedy algorithms?

A. They always fail for NP hard problem.<br>
B. They may not give the optimal solution for all problems.<br>
C. They are faster than dynamic programming in most cases.<br>
D. They make local choices without looking ahead.

## Q2 - Options
(A) A, C Only
(B) B, C Only
(C) A, B, C, D
(D) B, D Only

## Q2 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Greedy Algorithms & Dynamic Programming
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q80

A limitation is a genuine weakness of a technique, which rules out any statement that instead describes an advantage or makes an overstated claim.

- **A. They always fail for NP hard problem.** — wrong, greedy algorithms do not always fail on NP-hard problems, they often give fast approximate solutions and in special cases even exact optimal ones.
- **B. They may not give the optimal solution for all problems.** — correct, greedy algorithms optimize locally at each step, and that local view can miss the true global optimum, which is exactly why they are not always correct.
- **C. They are faster than dynamic programming in most cases.** — wrong as a limitation, speed relative to dynamic programming is an advantage of greedy methods, not a weakness.
- **D. They make local choices without looking ahead.** — correct, this short-sightedness is the structural reason greedy solutions can end up suboptimal.

The genuine limitations are B and D only.

## Q6

## Q6 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Greedy Algorithms & Dynamic Programming
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2025 (26 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q66

Dijkstra greedily fixes the smallest tentative distance, Kruskal greedily adds the cheapest edge that avoids a cycle, and Huffman greedily combines the two least-frequent nodes. Bellman-Ford repeatedly relaxes edges and is not a greedy algorithm.

## Q9
Given six weights 4,15,25,5,8,16 construct a 2-T tree. What is the minimum weighted path length?

## Q9 - Options
(A) 231
(B) 172
(C) 73
(D) 77

## Q9 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Greedy Algorithms & Dynamic Programming
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q27

The minimum weighted path length for a set of leaf weights is found by repeatedly merging the two smallest available weights and adding their sum to a running total, exactly as in building a Huffman tree.

Sorted weights: 4, 5, 8, 15, 16, 25

Merge 4+5=9, running total 9. Remaining: 8, 9, 15, 16, 25

Merge 8+9=17, running total 9+17=26. Remaining: 15, 16, 17, 25

Merge 15+16=31, running total 26+31=57. Remaining: 17, 25, 31

Merge 17+25=42, running total 57+42=99. Remaining: 31, 42

Merge 31+42=73, running total 99+73=172

The final running total, 172, is the minimum weighted path length, matching option B.

## Q10
Match List I with List II.

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| A. 8-Queens problem | I. Divide and conquer |
| B. Closest Pair of Points | II. Dynamic Programming |
| C. String Edit problem | III. Greedy Method |
| D. Knapsack problem | IV. Backtracking |

## Q10 - Options
(A) A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV
(B) A-I, B-IV, C-II, D-III
(C) A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III
(D) A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I

## Q10 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Greedy Algorithms & Dynamic Programming
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q71

Each classic algorithmic problem is matched to its standard textbook design paradigm.

The 8-Queens problem is the textbook example of backtracking, incrementally placing queens and undoing a placement when it leads to conflict, giving A-IV.

The Closest Pair of Points problem is solved in O(n log n) by recursively splitting the point set and combining results, the classic divide and conquer pattern, giving B-I.

The String Edit (edit distance) problem is solved by building up a table of optimal subproblem solutions, the defining trait of dynamic programming, giving C-II.

The Knapsack problem, in the form commonly paired with algorithm paradigms in this kind of list, is solved by repeatedly making the locally best choice, the Greedy Method, giving D-III.

This gives the mapping A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

## Q11
Find the optimal solution for the fractional knapsack problem when its maximum capacity is 15.

For a knapsack problem, P and W are profits and weights for a set of 7 items as given below:

P = {9, 5, 2, 7, 6, 16, 9}<br>
W = {2, 5, 6, 11, 1, 9, 3}

## Q11 - Options
(A) 43
(B) 40
(C) 45
(D) 44

## Q11 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Greedy Algorithms & Dynamic Programming
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q95

The fractional knapsack greedy strategy sorts items by profit-to-weight ratio and fills the capacity starting from the highest ratio.

Ratios: item1=9/2=4.5, item2=5/5=1, item3=2/6≈0.33, item4=7/11≈0.64, item5=6/1=6, item6=16/9≈1.78, item7=9/3=3

Sorted descending: item5 (6), item1 (4.5), item7 (3), item6 (1.78), item2 (1), item4 (0.64), item3 (0.33)

Filling capacity 15: take item5 fully (weight 1, value 6, capacity left 14), item1 fully (weight 2, value 9, capacity left 12), item7 fully (weight 3, value 9, capacity left 9), item6 fully (weight 9, value 16, capacity left 0)

Total value = 6+9+9+16 = 40, and capacity is now exhausted, so this is the optimal solution.

## Q12
What is the maximum value of items you can carry if the maximum weight allowed is 25 with a fractional knapsack?

For a knapsack problem, P and W are profits and weights for a set of 7 items as given below:

P = {9, 5, 2, 7, 6, 16, 9}<br>
W = {2, 5, 6, 11, 1, 9, 3}

## Q12 - Options
(A) 48.1
(B) 49
(C) 47.9
(D) 40

## Q12 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Greedy Algorithms & Dynamic Programming
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q96

Continuing the greedy fill in ratio order (item5, item1, item7, item6, item2, item4, item3) with a larger capacity of 25 lets more items fit before the capacity runs out.

Taking item5, item1, item7, item6, and item2 fully uses weight 1+2+3+9+5=20, contributing value 6+9+9+16+5=45, and leaves 25-20=5 units of capacity.

The next item in ratio order, item4 (weight 11, value 7), can only be partially added since just 5 units of capacity remain. Its fractional contribution is 7 × (5/11) ≈ 3.18

Total value ≈ 45 + 3.18 = 48.18, which rounds to approximately 48.1, the closest available option.

## Q13
If a new item (P=5, W=2) is added to the list, making the total items 8 and the capacity 25, then the best-case time of the fractional knapsack for this case is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

For a knapsack problem, P and W are profits and weights for a set of 7 items as given below:

P = {9, 5, 2, 7, 6, 16, 9}<br>
W = {2, 5, 6, 11, 1, 9, 3}

## Q13 - Options
(A) O(8)
(B) O(64)
(C) O(24)
(D) O(56)

## Q13 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Greedy Algorithms & Dynamic Programming
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q97

The fractional knapsack algorithm's running time is dominated by sorting the n items by profit-to-weight ratio, giving a time complexity of O(n log n).

With n=8 items after adding the new one, evaluating this bound numerically gives n log₂n = 8 × log₂8 = 8 × 3 = 24

This matches O(24), while O(8) understates the sorting cost, and O(64) and O(56) do not correspond to the n log n evaluation at n=8.

## Q14
The most efficient solution for the fractional knapsack problem with maximum capacity 15 can be obtained by using\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

For a knapsack problem, P and W are profits and weights for a set of 7 items as given below:

P = {9, 5, 2, 7, 6, 16, 9}<br>
W = {2, 5, 6, 11, 1, 9, 3}

## Q14 - Options
(A) Divide and Conquer
(B) Dynamic Programming
(C) Greedy Algorithm
(D) Backtracking

## Q14 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Greedy Algorithms & Dynamic Programming
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q98

Fractional knapsack allows items to be split into any proportion, which means the locally optimal choice of always taking the item with the highest available profit-to-weight ratio next never has to be reconsidered later.

This greedy-choice property is exactly what makes a Greedy Algorithm both correct and efficient for fractional knapsack, unlike 0/1 knapsack, where indivisible items break this property and require dynamic programming instead.

Divide and conquer and backtracking are not the standard efficient approaches for this problem, since neither matches its greedy-choice structure.

Which of the following statements is correct for a knapsack?

For a knapsack problem, P and W are profits and weights for a set of 7 items as given below:

P = {9, 5, 2, 7, 6, 16, 9}<br>

## Q15 - Options
(A) 0/1 knapsack can be applied for all kinds of problems but fractional knapsack can be applied only if the problem meets certain conditions.
(B) There is no difference between the two. They give the same solution for any problem.
(C) We use greedy algorithm for 0/1 knapsack and dynamic programming for fractional knapsack.
(D) In 0/1 knapsack problem, items cannot be divided into smaller portions and in fractional knapsack we can divide the item into required proportions of weight.

## Q15 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Greedy Algorithms & Dynamic Programming
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q99

The defining difference between the two knapsack variants is divisibility. In the 0/1 knapsack problem, each item must be taken whole or left out entirely, while in the fractional knapsack problem, any item can be split into whatever proportion of its weight is needed to fill the remaining capacity.

This divisibility difference is also why the two problems need different solution techniques. Fractional knapsack's divisibility gives it the greedy-choice property, which a Greedy Algorithm exploits directly, while 0/1 knapsack's indivisibility breaks that property and requires Dynamic Programming instead, the reverse pairing of what option C claims. The two problems can also give different optimal values on the same input, so they are not equivalent in general, ruling out options A and B.

## Q16
Consider the following statements:

A. The running time of dynamic programming algorithm is alway θ(p) where p is number of subproblems.<br>
B. When a recurrence relation has cyclic dependency, it is impossible to use that recurrence relation (unmodified) in a correct dynamic program.<br>
C. For a dynamic programming algorithm, computing all values in a bottom-up fashion is asymptotically faster than using recursion and memorization.<br>
D. If a problem X can be reduced to a known NP-hard problem, then X must be NP-hard.

Which of the statement(s) is (are) true?

## Q16 - Options
(A) Only B and A
(B) Only B
(C) Only B and C
(D) Only B and D

## Q16 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Greedy Algorithms & Dynamic Programming
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2019 (4 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q1

Evaluating each statement regarding dynamic programming and complexity:

- **A** — false. The total running time of a dynamic programming algorithm is the sum of times across all subproblems, which is θ(p × t) where t is the time needed to compute each subproblem, not simply θ(p).
- **B** — correct. Dynamic programming requires subproblem dependencies to form a directed acyclic graph. Cyclic dependencies create circular references that cannot be evaluated without modifying the recurrence.
- **C** — false. Bottom-up tabulation and top-down memoization share the exact same asymptotic complexity θ(p × t), differing only in recursion-call overhead and constant factors.
- **D** — false. Reducing X to an NP-hard problem only proves that X is no harder than that problem. To establish NP-hardness for X, the reduction must be directed from a known NP-hard problem to X.

## Q17
Consider the following steps:<br>
S₁: Characterize the structure of an optimal solution<br>
S₂: Compute the value of an optimal solution in bottom-up fashion

Which of the step(s) is/are common to both dynamic programming and greedy algorithms?

## Q17 - Options
(A) Only S₁
(B) Only S₂
(C) Both S₁ and S₂
(D) Neither S₁ nor S₂

## Q17 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Greedy Algorithms & Dynamic Programming
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2019 (24 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q45

Comparing algorithm design paradigms:

- **S1 (Characterize optimal solution structure)** is required by both dynamic programming and greedy algorithms because both require the problem to exhibit optimal substructure.
- **S2 (Bottom-up computation)** is unique to dynamic programming, which solves and stores overlapping subproblems from the base cases upward. Greedy algorithms instead make top-down iterative choices without solving subproblems bottom-up.

Therefore, only step S1 is common to both.

## Q18
Consider two sequences X and Y :

X = &lt;0, 1, 2, 1, 3, 0, 1&gt;<br>
Y = &lt;1, 3, 2, 0, 1, 0&gt;

The length of longest common subsequence between X and Y is

## Q18 - Options
(A) 2
(B) 3
(C) 5
(D) 4

## Q18 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Greedy Algorithms & Dynamic Programming
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2018 (20 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q20

Dynamic programming establishes that the maximum length of a common subsequence between X and Y is 4.

- Let X = &lt;0, 1, 2, 1, 3, 0, 1&gt; and Y = &lt;1, 3, 2, 0, 1, 0&gt;.
- One common subsequence of length 4 is &lt;1, 2, 0, 1&gt;:<br>
    In X: index 1 ('1'), index 2 ('2'), index 5 ('0'), index 6 ('1').<br>
    In Y: index 0 ('1'), index 2 ('2'), index 3 ('0'), index 4 ('1').
- Another common subsequence of length 4 is &lt;1, 3, 0, 1&gt;.
- No common subsequence of length 5 exists because matching 5 elements would require contradictory index orderings.
- Therefore, the length is 4 (Option D).
